\chapter{How It Feels}
\label{ch:ta-how-it-feels}
\hlchaptermodality{72}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name anger, fear and sorrow in Tamil, and say to laugh and to cry.}

Complete TA-C72-cry and say all five words of the chapter in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kōpam]{\ta{கோபம்} (kōpam) — anger}

\label{lesson:TA-C72-anger}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{viḷaiyāḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கோபம்}}
\textbf{\ta{கோபம்}} (\emph{kōpam}) — \textquotedblleft{}anger\textquotedblright{}.

Anger — the ordinary everyday word for it, not a literary one.

You can read all of it already, and one part of it you only just learned: \textbf{\ta{கோ}} is \ta{க} with the \ta{◌ோ} sign, the sign whose free-standing letter \ta{ஓ} you met last chapter.

It ends in \textbf{\ta{ம்}}, like \ta{வணக்கம்}, \ta{தூக்கம்} and \ta{பணம்} before it. That ending is now four words deep, and it is a good bet for a Tamil noun.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five feelings.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kōpam}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{கோபம்}}, and point at the sign of the letter you met last chapter
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{paṇam}, then \emph{kōpam}, and name the ending they share
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kaḻuvu}, then say \emph{viḷaiyāḍu}, then say \emph{kōpam}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mēsai}, then read \textbf{\ta{எழு}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{கோபம்} mean, and which sign is on its first letter? (\textquotedblleft{}Anger\textquotedblright{}; the \textbf{\ta{ோ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[payam]{\ta{பயம்} (payam) — fear}

\label{lesson:TA-C72-fear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kōpam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{பயம்}}
\textbf{\ta{பயம்}} (\emph{payam}) — \textquotedblleft{}fear\textquotedblright{}.

Fear.

Three letters and not one vowel sign anywhere: \ta{ப}, \ta{ய}, and \ta{ம} with a \ta{புள்ளி}. Every letter is carrying its own built-in \emph{a}, which is the plainest a Tamil word can possibly be written.

It ends in the same \textbf{\ta{ம்}} as \ta{கோபம்}, which is not a coincidence — Tamil keeps a whole shelf of feeling-nouns with that ending.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and both of them end the same way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{payam}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kōpam}, then \emph{payam} — and say what both endings have in common
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{viḷaiyāḍu}, then say \emph{kōpam}, then say \emph{payam}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{கட்டில்}}, then say \emph{tūṅgu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many vowel signs does \ta{பயம்} carry? (\textbf{None} — every letter keeps its built-in \emph{a}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[payam]{\ta{பயம்} — a word with no vowel signs}

\label{lesson:TA-W27-read-payam}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: you can say \emph{kōpam} and \emph{payam}. Now read the second one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{பயம்} — a word with no vowel signs}
Every word you have read so far carried at least one sign. \textbf{\ta{பயம்}} carries none, and that makes it the clearest possible demonstration of what a bare Tamil letter is worth.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{ப}} & \emph{pa} & no sign — the letter's own built-in \emph{a} is the vowel \\
\textbf{\ta{ய}} & \emph{ya} & the same again \\
\textbf{\ta{ம்}} & \emph{m} & \ta{ம} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}}, so no vowel at all \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ப} · \ta{ய} · \ta{ம்} $\to$ \ta{பயம்}}
\end{quote}

So a Tamil consonant is never really silent by default. It says \emph{a} unless something stops it, and the only thing that stops it is the dot. Read the word once and hear the two \emph{a} sounds you were never told about.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ப}} — then \textbf{\ta{ய}} — then \textbf{\ta{ம்}}
  \item \emph{Point to:} the one mark in the whole word, and say what it does
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{பயம்}}, then \textbf{\ta{கடை}}, and say which one needed a sign
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kōpam}, then say \emph{payam}, then read \textbf{\ta{பயம்}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{பயம்}}. Which vowel do \ta{ப} and \ta{ய} carry, and why is none written? (\emph{\textbf{a}} — it is built into the letter.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[varuttam]{\ta{வருத்தம்} (varuttam) — sorrow, regret}

\label{lesson:TA-C72-sorrow}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: read \textbf{\ta{பயம்}}, and say what it means.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வருத்தம்}}
\textbf{\ta{வருத்தம்}} (\emph{varuttam}) — \textquotedblleft{}sorrow, regret\textquotedblright{}.

One word for both kinds of sorry: sad \textbf{about} something, and sorry \textbf{for} something.

This is the word that finishes an apology in ordinary speech. You already have \ta{தவறு} (\emph{tavaṟu}), the mistake, and \ta{மன்னிக்கவும்} (\emph{maṉṉikkavum}), which asks formally to be forgiven. \ta{வருத்தம்} sits between them: it names the feeling rather than making the request, and it is the one you can say to a friend without sounding like a letter.

Its middle is a doubled \textbf{\ta{த்த}}, the same closing-and-leaning you read in \ta{சட்டை} and \ta{வண்டி}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three feelings, and one of them is an apology.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{varuttam}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tavaṟu}, then \emph{varuttam} — the mistake, then the feeling about it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maṉṉikkavum}, then \emph{varuttam}, and say which is the formal one
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{payam}, then read \textbf{\ta{பயம்}}, then say \emph{varuttam}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{suvar}, then read \textbf{\ta{ஓடு}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two would you say to a friend — \ta{மன்னிக்கவும்} or \ta{வருத்தம்}? (\textbf{\ta{வருத்தம்}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[siri]{\ta{சிரி} (siri) — to laugh}

\label{lesson:TA-C72-laugh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{varuttam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சிரி}}
\textbf{\ta{சிரி}} (\emph{siri}) — \textquotedblleft{}to laugh\textquotedblright{}.

To laugh.

Two letters, both wearing the same \textbf{\ta{ி}} sign — \ta{ச} and \ta{ர}, each with the short \emph{i}. Words that repeat a sign like that are easy to read and easy to say, and this is a good one to read aloud before you meet its opposite.

After three nouns, this is a verb: something a person \textbf{does}, not something they have.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the feelings start doing something.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{siri}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{சிரி}}, and point at the sign that appears twice
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kōpam}, then \emph{siri} — and say which one is a verb
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{பயம்}}, then say \emph{varuttam}, then say \emph{siri}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{தரை}}, then say \emph{kaḻuvu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{சிரி} mean, and which sign does it carry twice? (\textquotedblleft{}To laugh\textquotedblright{}; the \textbf{\ta{ி}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aḻu]{\ta{அழு} (aḻu) — to cry}

\label{lesson:TA-C72-cry}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{siri} mean, and what did \emph{payam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அழு}}
\textbf{\ta{அழு}} (\emph{aḻu}) — \textquotedblleft{}to cry\textquotedblright{}.

To cry — the mirror of the verb before it, and just as short.

It opens on \ta{அ}, the free-standing letter, because the word begins with that vowel: the same pattern you saw when \ta{ஓ} opened \ta{ஓடு}. And in the middle is \textbf{\ta{ழ}} again, the third time you have met it after \ta{தமிழ்} and \ta{கழுவு}.

Five feelings now: three you can have — \ta{கோபம்}, \ta{பயம்}, \ta{வருத்தம்} — and two you can do, \ta{சிரி} and \ta{அழு}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: three nouns and two verbs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aḻu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{siri}, then \emph{aḻu} — the pair, one after the other
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five — \emph{kōpam}, \emph{payam}, \emph{varuttam}, \emph{siri}, \emph{aḻu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{varuttam}, then say \emph{siri}, then say \emph{aḻu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kūrai}, then read \textbf{\ta{விளையாடு}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three of the five are things you \textbf{have}, and which two are things you \textbf{do}? (\textbf{\ta{கோபம்}, \ta{பயம்}, \ta{வருத்தம்}}; \textbf{\ta{சிரி}, \ta{அழு}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
